title: Beyond Extremes: Asymmetric Coupling Strength and Sensitivity of Global Vegetation Productivity to Precipitation
content:
Abstract

Precipitation is a primary driver of terrestrial vegetation productivity, and their coupling reflects key carbon-water interactions in ecosystems. While asymmetric productivity responses to extreme precipitation anomalies are recognized, it remains unknown whether fundamental ecosystem indicators like coupling strength (the correlation between productivity and precipitation) and response sensitivity (the regression slope) are also asymmetric under non-extreme conditions. Here, using multi-source remote sensing proxies and precipitation records, we constructed three asymmetric indices based on extreme values, coupling strength (correlation coefficients), and sensitivity (regression slopes) to systematically evaluate their global spatiotemporal patterns. We found that 41.4% of global vegetated areas exhibit significant asymmetry (with 19.4% remaining robustly asymmetric even after strictly filtering out the impact of observation noise). Although negative asymmetry generally dominates (∼70% overall, and >80% within the strictly noise-filtered domain), striking divergences in both direction and magnitude emerge among the indices. Over the past four decades, ∼12% of vegetated lands (predominantly grasslands) exhibited a shift toward greater symmetry, driven by disproportionately enhanced vegetation sensitivity during wet years. These findings redefine our understanding of non-linear vegetation-precipitation interactions, providing critical insights for land managers to optimize drought mitigation and for climate modelers to refine carbon sequestration projections.
